verdictReason: Killed. The licence is no moat: Oregon needs a 5-day course, no experience, a $97.50 fee (D15, D16); Marin Water lists 63 testers from 34 firms (D17); ECUA lists ~57 (SVC2-E5). Utility contracts are experience-weighted and contested (EWEB: experience 40 of 100 pts, 3 bidders, ~$50k/yr, D1-D2; Fresno 2023: ~1,800 assemblies, 7 bids, D5-D6). Bottom-up profit is ~$19.1k (~$10/h); pessimistic is about -$6.3k, and break-even there needs ~1,000 baseline tests, a 1988-established firm's volume (D30).

answers.question: Can a new certified tester win utility-run testing contracts at a size that makes the route worth more than a job?
answers.answer: No evidence that a first-year stranger can. Contracts that exist are small, contested and experience-weighted. EWEB (Eugene) awarded one contractor a 5-year $250,000 program (about $50k a year) covering ~800 enrolled commercial customers plus non-compliant ones; three bidders were scored on Experience 40, Resources and Responsiveness 35, Pricing 25, and the winner offered the lowest average rate ($68 vs $99 and $171). Fresno's 2023 contract (~1,800 assemblies, up to $165,900 a year, about $92 per assembly) drew seven bids and went to an established Pasadena engineering firm; its 2015 contract was $66,000 for ~1,600 devices with four bids. Medford Water drew a single bid ($185,212.03) although at least four backflow firms pulled the documents. Kitsap's 2026 RFP requires three client references. Even a won EWEB-sized contract is a labor-bound wage of about $50k gross, not a scalable business.

answers.question: Is the tester certification a barrier that excludes competitors?
answers.answer: No. Oregon requires an approved 5-day tester course, lists no experience requirement, and charges a $97.50 certification fee; the licence is required only to test for a fee. One California district (Marin Water) lists 63 testers from 34 organizations and disclaims any quality control, ECUA lists ~57 companies, and a working tester says many local certifiers are weekend workers. Only Texas adds a two-year experience hurdle (SVC2-E2), which makes a stranger's entry harder there, not easier elsewhere.

answers.question: Do free or cheap alternatives already cover the annual-agreement wedge (test, report filing, next-year scheduling)?
answers.answer: Largely yes. Utilities themselves send due and overdue notices to owners and run the reporting platform (Sugar Land: BSI Online, with testers filing within 48 hours; Longmont: SwiftComply). Testers can buy scheduling, routing and reminder software (Syncta, price unpublished). Some utilities offer a city-contracted tester at a fixed fee on the utility bill (Longmont $137.50 per assembly). Owners may delegate testing to tenants, site managers or property managers. The scheduling and filing chore is therefore a utility-subsidised, low-value add-on, not an exclusive wedge.

answers.question: What does the first-365-days bottom-up economics look like for the reference entrant, and does it survive the pessimistic case?
answers.answer: Baseline (all inputs below are sourced or labelled assumption): 400 tests x $110 = $44,000 revenue; variable $45 per visit x 400 = $18,000 plus fixed $6,923 = $24,923 cost; profit about $19,077 over roughly 1,820 owner hours (about $10.5 per hour). Pessimistic (price x0.8 = $88, volume x0.5 = 200, cost x1.5): revenue $17,600, cost $23,884.50, profit about -$6,285. Break-even under pessimistic price and cost needs about 507 tests, i.e. roughly 1,000 baseline tests in year one, equal to the annual volume of a firm testing since 1988. Upfront cash before first revenue is about $3,448 (about $5,172 at x1.5), above the $4,500 startup cash in the pessimistic case. Sensitivity: even at a baseline of 600 tests the pessimistic profit is about -$4,235 with these fixed costs.

answers.question: Is there evidence of unmet demand a new tester could fill?
answers.answer: Only transient surges. A 2016 Idaho local news report quotes a specialist saying many testers were too swamped to answer the phone after one city began citywide enforcement, with backlogs up to three months in some places. Demand is real and recurring (owners must pay for an annual test, utilities enforce it), but pricing evidence shows heavy compression and low-cost, uninsured competitors, and purveyors send notices to owners, not testers, so the entrant has no list of leads.

answers.question: What licence, insurance and platform constraints apply?
answers.answer: State certification (Oregon 5-day course, $97.50; Texas adds two years of experience), local approved-tester lists with insurance minimums ($500,000 combined single limit at Lincoln, Nebraska; $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 aggregate in Kitsap County's contract), reference requirements in RFPs, and mandatory submission of reports to utility platforms (BSI Online within 48 hours at Sugar Land; a $10 per passing test portal charge at Longmont whose payer the page does not state).

killReasons.reason: The tester licence is not a barrier: Oregon needs an approved 5-day course, lists no experience requirement and charges $97.50; a single California district lists 63 testers from 34 organizations and disclaims quality control, and price competition from low-cost part-time testers is documented. There is no exclusive or compounding edge, and a rival could copy the entrant by taking a one-week course.

The utility-contract route cited as the only structural edge is not open to a first-year stranger: EWEB scores Experience 40 of 100 points and Qualifications and Experience is 30% at Kitsap with three client references required; Fresno's 1,800-assembly contract drew seven bids and went to an established firm; the EWEB winner also had the lowest rate. No source shows a first-year entrant winning such a contract.

Bottom-up economics fail the pessimistic case: baseline profit is about $19,077 for about 1,820 hours (about $10.5 per hour); pessimistic profit is about -$6,285 and break-even there needs roughly 1,000 baseline tests in year one, the annual volume of a firm testing since 1988. Upfront cash also exceeds $4,500 at x1.5 cost.

The annual-agreement wedge (reminders, filing, scheduling) is already supplied by utilities, which mail due and overdue notices to owners and run the reporting platform, plus tester software; a city-contracted tester at a fixed fee is also offered on the utility bill. The entrant cannot exclusively own the scheduling or filing step.
Labor-bound field service: a solo tester completes about 8 to 12 tests a day on a tight route, so profit scales with owner hours, not with the business.

State and local registration, insurance minimums ($500,000 at Lincoln; $1M/$2M at Kitsap) and utility-specific portals or per-test charges add friction and fixed cost for each new service area; Texas adds a two-year experience requirement.

assumptions: Entrant is a stranger in an open-entry state (Oregon-style: 5-day course, no experience requirement); start-up cash $4,500, first revenue about day 75, 35 owner hours per week (about 1,820 hours in 365 days).

Volume 400 paid tests in year one (assumption): roughly 80 to 100 commercial assemblies a month in the last quarter via cold outreach to property managers and plumber referrals; capacity of 8 to 12 tests a day is not the constraint, customer acquisition is. A 600-test sensitivity gives baseline profit about $32,077 but pessimistic about -$4,235.

Price $110 per test (assumption inside sourced ranges: $85-$180 commercial per SVC2-E1, $100-$300+ commercial and $70-$150 residential per D29, average RPZ about $100 per D19, $137.50 city-contracted in Longmont per D13).
Variable cost $45 per visit (assumption at the midpoint of the $35 to $55 per-visit cost in D21, which excludes the owner's own pay).

Fixed costs $6,923: course $850 (D25 $600-$1,000), certification fee $98 (D16), gauge kit $1,200 (assumption within D25 range $500-$2,600), liability and commercial auto insurance $1,000 (D22 $500-$1,500), gauge calibration $75, business formation and licence $300 (assumption), scheduling software $600 (assumption, price unpublished D24), marketing $1,500 (assumption), portal charges $1,000 (assumption: $10 per test on a quarter of tests, per D14, payer unstated), bookkeeping $300 (assumption).
Pessimistic case applies price x0.8 ($88), volume x0.5 (200 tests) and cost x1.5 to both per-visit ($67.50) and fixed costs ($10,384.50): revenue $17,600, cost $23,884.50, profit -$6,284.50.
No utility-run contract is assumed won in year one (D1, D6, D27); winning an EWEB-sized program (about $50k a year, D2) would not change the labor-bound nature.
Upfront outlay before first revenue about $3,448 (course, certification, gauge, insurance, formation), about $5,172 at x1.5, which exceeds the $4,500 start-up cash.

legalNotes: Paid testing requires state or local certification: Oregon certifies after an approved 5-day course (license needed to test for a fee), Texas TCEQ adds two years of experience (SVC2-E2), Lincoln NE requires a Grade VI tester certificate with renewal letter (D26). The entrant must pick one open-entry jurisdiction and cannot sell across state lines on one licence.

Utilities may require tester registration, gauge calibration records and liability insurance (Lincoln: $500,000 combined single limit; Kitsap sample contract: $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 aggregate) and may remove testers who omit documents.

Reports must go through the utility's platform (BSI Online within 48 hours at Sugar Land; SwiftComply with a $10 per passing test charge at Longmont) and fire-line devices in Texas are restricted to state-licensed testers employed by a fireline testing company, per Sugar Land.

Public bids are won on stated criteria that include references and experience (Kitsap needs three recent client references); no legal barrier to bidding exists, but a new firm may not meet the qualification weighting.
Research used only public pages read normally with no logins, contact or purchases; no ToS issues arise for the proposed business beyond the licensing and insurance items above.
unverified: Quotes were taken from the page text returned by the fetch tool; a direct download of the EWEB and Medford PDFs was blocked by the proxy and was not circumvented, so wording was not re-checked against the raw files.

EWEB bid table unit is shown as 'Average Rate' and the reader described it as hourly; the page also names the contractor both 'Eugene Backflow Testing' and 'Eugene Backflow Services', which may or may not be the same firm.

Medford contract term, whether the sole bidder (Rogue Valley Backflow Service) is the incumbent, and whether the contract was awarded are not confirmed; South Jordan term and number of bidders are not stated on the page; Fresno 2023 'seven bids' and the 'four finalists' come from the reader's summary of the page.
Marin Water count of 63 testers from 34 organizations is the reader's count of the table.
Who pays the $10 SwiftComply charge at Longmont (tester or customer) is not stated; Syncta pricing is not published.
Highlands Ranch Water's price for commercial devices (SVC2-E3) remains unpublished; the HeatingHelp thread is undated and its $12.50 per test city-contract anecdote is a forum claim.
Volume of 400 tests in year one, the marketing spend and the customer-acquisition rate are assumptions; no source shows what a first-year stranger actually sells.
A retailer page listed a Watts TK-99E test kit at $4,298.52 (sold out); it was treated as an outlier and not used. Gauge price rests on vendor and secondary guides ($500-$2,600).
No evidence either way on whether property managers pay more for a bundled annual agreement than for single tests.
nextStep: None; revisit only if a documented case shows a first-year tester winning a utility-run program, or a property-management firm commits in writing to 200+ assemblies a year.
